National Weather Service Burlington VT

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 226 AM EDT Friday...

No significant changes were made to the forecast.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 226 AM EDT Friday...

1. A cold front will pass through the region today with 
associated light showers. The front clears the area this 
afternoon/evening with clearing skies, as high pressure builds 
in for the weekend.

2. Brief high pressure will break down Monday night, and give 
way to rounds of rain.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 226 AM EDT Friday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: A cold front will move through the region today with 
some light associated rain showers. The front at the time of this 
forecast is just entering the St. Lawrence Valley. Southwesterly 
flow is driving some lake enhanced showers and clouds downstream of 
Lake Ontario into portions of southern St. Lawrence County in New 
York. The front will gradually shift east this morning through 
northern New York and into Vermont just after sunrise. A few 
isolated showers will be possible with the front, especially in the 
Northeast Kingdom, where some better convergence will be located. 
Moisture will be lacking with the front due to convection yesterday. 
As the front moves east towards the Connecticut River, some 
diurnally driven instability could be enough to generate some 
isolated rumbles of thunder, though chances for any stronger storms 
are low to none. High temperatures today will be tricky with the 
frontal passage in addition to normal diurnal heating. Though with 
cooling flow aloft, and winds turning northwest, highs in the raw 
model guidance show cooler trends with high only in the upper 60s to 
low 70s. Highs in south and eastern Vermont may remain on the warmer 
side into the mid to upper 70s, to near 80 with the front reaching 
them later in the day today. As the front clears the area by 
tomorrow afternoon/evening, much drier and cooler air will filter in 
overnight. Strong radiational cooling is anticipated tonight with 
temperature outside of Lake Champlain falling well into the low to 
mid 40s. Localized sub 40 temperatures may be possible in the 
coldest hollows of the Adirondacks. Friday night will see high 
probabilities for valley fog with many locations falling below 
crossover temperatures under clearing skies.

High pressure will build in on Saturday with mainly clear skies 
aside from fair weather cumulus in the higher terrain. Some light 
breezes from southwest channeled flow in the St. Lawrence Valley to 
10 mph will be possible as well. Highs will be relatively seasonable 
in the mid 70s. High pressure will dip south on Sunday as a cold 
front will sink south from Quebec. Zonal flow ahead of a positively 
tilted shortwave will keep moisture fairly progressive, but some 
shower activity will be possible near the International Border by 
mid to late Sunday. Lifting along the front with cool temperatures 
aloft may lead to some weak instability on the southern periphery of 
the front in northern Vermont and near the US-11 corridor in 
northern New York. The front then stalls out across the region 
becoming oriented northwest to southeast Sunday night, setting the 
stage for a more active weather pattern heading into next week.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Over Monday night into Tuesday, surface high pressure 
centered north of Montreal will begin to shift east. A humid air 
mass will amble east in response to a 500mb high around 595 dam 
builds into the southeastern US. Various vorts picked up from the 
tropical Pacific will round the ridge axis while a compact upper low 
tracks east across Canada. Moisture will overrun the dry air left in 
the wake of surface high pressure along Sunday's front just to our 
south. The boundary appears likely to waffle around the region as 
surface high pressure redevelops across the Canadian maritimes and 
helps slow things up a bit. The weather system translating east 
across Canada will start to move east of our area after Wednesday, 
which will then drag a cold front southeast next Thursday. Secondary 
cyclogenesis appears likely across coastal Maine, and the slow 
moving nature of the system could allow some additional showers to 
linger into Friday until the backside of the longwave trough ambles 
east.

Some uncertainty remains on the exact placement of heavier swaths of 
rain along the waffling boundary. Ensemble means and probabilities 
suggest that the highest rainfall totals will have a greater 
probability south. Between Monday and Thursday, probabilities of 1 
(30-40%) and 2" (~10%) over the 72 hour time frame are relatively 
unchanged from yesterday. Cluster analysis does show some spread in 
where the highest rainfall amounts could be, and so we'll continue 
to closely monitor how this pattern evolves.

&&

.AVIATION /12Z FRIDAY THROUGH TUESDAY/...
Through 12Z Saturday...Not much has changed over the last few
hours. Timing of lower ceilings along and behind the front have
been a bit slower than initially presented. There are pockets 
of clouds located around 1500-3500 ft agl across the region and
patchy fog in southern and eastern Vermont impacting KMPV at
this time. The front is northwest of KSLK and KPBG with a few
showers. Used PROB30s with some increasing coverage as the front
reaches east into Vermont about 14z-19z. Some MVFR ceilings 
could still take place with the front, with terminals trending 
VFR after 19z. Wind speeds are currently around 5 knots or less 
and will increase to 7 to 10 knots with a few gusts 15 to 18 
knots. Skies will trend clear and winds will decrease beyond 00z
Saturday with some patchy fog development.

Outlook...

Saturday: VFR. Patchy BR.
Saturday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Sunday: VFR. Chance SHRA, Slight chance TSRA.
Sunday Night: VFR. Slight chance SHRA, Slight chance TSRA.
Monday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Monday Night: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Slight chance
SHRA.
Tuesday: Mainly MVFR, with local IFR possible. Chance SHRA,
Slight chance TSRA.
